blocks.text: The chapter begins by making return to Jehovah its interpretive threshold. The people are warned not to repeat their ancestors’ refusal to heed earlier prophets. Their ancestors and the prophets themselves have passed away, but the prophetic words proved effective: they “overtook” those who ignored them. That opening explains why the following visions are not detached images; they follow a call to reckon honestly with the past and to return.

The dated setting introduces a sequence of visions. In the first, a horseman and colored horses report that the earth is quiet, while an angel asks when mercy will come to Jerusalem and Judah. The answer joins comfort for Jerusalem with displeasure toward nations at ease and promises that the house will be built and Jerusalem restored. The final vision uses horns for powers that scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem, and smiths for agents who will terrify and cast down those powers. The text identifies their broad roles, but it does not name four uncontested empires for the four horns.

sections.title: Visions of Jerusalem and Its Oppressors
